summary: A description of the user-side Telnet program built into UCSB's Online System. It lets a terminal on that system act like an ordinary teletype and log in to other time-sharing hosts across the ARPANET. It covers how to start it, the virtual teletype, how to return to it, and what happens on network errors.

eli5.summary: It is like a telephone that lets you call a faraway computer and type to it as if you were sitting right there. This note explains how to dial and what to do if the call goes wrong.

how do you map between different keyboards
how does ucsb user telnet handle display
subtitle: Using remote time-sharing systems from a local terminal via the network

tldr.problem: Users at UCSB's Online System (OLS) had terminals very different from teletypes; they needed a way to access remote time-sharing systems on the ARPANET while mapping their unfamiliar keyboard and display to what the remote system expected.
tldr.mechanism: A User TELNET program runs on the user's local system and maps their keyboard to a virtual teletype character set (7-bit ASCII), then maps output from the remote system back to displayable characters on their storage scope. Server TELNET at the remote site performs the inverse mapping.
tldr.outcome: This was an early implementation of interactive remote terminal access. TELNET evolved into the standard protocol, but this 1971 implementation shows how the concept worked in practice.

facts.label: Author
facts.value: J. White, UCSB Computer Research Lab

today: This 1971 description of User TELNET is an early real-world implementation of the TELNET concept. TELNET eventually became a standard protocol (now governed by RFC 854 and later RFCs). The character-level translation approach shown here evolved into the telnet protocol that became ubiquitous on the Internet.

sections.title: The User TELNET Concept
sections.content:
RFC 206 describes a User TELNET program implemented in UCSB's Online System (OLS) by Mark Krilanovich. It allows an OLS user to dial up a remote time-sharing system on the ARPANET and use it as if directly connected.

The User TELNET works together with a Server TELNET at the remote site. Both programs translate between their local keyboard and display hardware and a standard virtual teletype using 7-bit ASCII. For UCSB, this is critical because OLS terminals are not teletypes and have different key layouts and character capabilities. User TELNET masks this difference and makes the ARPANET transparent to the user.
sections.eli5: User TELNET is a bridge: it takes your special keyboard and screen and makes them look like a normal teletype to the remote computer.

sections.title: Character Mapping and Display
sections.content:
The virtual teletype uses a 7-bit ASCII character set. User TELNET maps OLS keyboard keys to virtual teletype characters; for example, pressing 'LF' on the virtual teletype can be done with SUB, CASE J, or [1] on the OLS keyboard. Similarly, CASE substitutes for the CTRL key; pressing CASE and C in sequence produces control-C.

Display transformation is more complex. OLS storage scopes cannot show lowercase letters, so User TELNET maps all lowercase alphabetics to uppercase before displaying. Special characters like ENQ, ACK, BEL and NAK are displayed in a reserved two-line field at the top of the screen, so the user can see important status signals.
sections.eli5: Keyboard keys map to virtual keys, and incoming letters are adjusted to show on the screen. Special signals go to the top.

sections.title: Network Sites and Connection
sections.content:
User TELNET knows about fifteen ARPANET sites at launch: UCLA, SRI, UCSB, Utah, BBN, MIT, RAND, SDC, Harvard, Lincoln, Stanford, Illinois, CASE, Carnegie-Mellon and Burroughs (Illiac IV). Each site has a decimal site number. The user specifies the site number and the Server TELNET socket number (usually 1) to establish a duplex connection.

Once connected, the user logs in using the remote system's conventions. The remote system sends its login prompt, and the user types their credentials. From that point, the user can interact with the remote time-sharing system as if sitting at its console.
sections.eli5: You pick a site from a list and a port, and the connection opens. Then you log in and use the faraway computer as if you were there.
